Mother-of-four Jacinta Bathalda, 35, from Little Hulton, Salford, was awoken at 03:00 BST on 10 August by her son's shouts and was horrified to see someone stealing her car. Sceptical when the police told her they were looking for the vehicle, she was inspired to search for it herself when a friend asked if the Audi had a tracker. She was alerted to the manufacturer's app by a friend who worked for Audi, and was amazed five days after the theft when it informed her the car was low on petrol. She and her family then drove to an address 30 miles away in Blackburn, where the app said the car was. Image source, CCTV Image caption, Jacinta Bathalda obtained CCTV of her car black in east Lancashire At first she drew a blank, but after asking round in the neighbourhood one person sent her a video of her car with new number plates fitted. "I was so shocked," Bathalda said, adding a DVLA check revealed the plates were for a Volkswagen. Later that day, the app revealed another location 20 minutes away in Colne, where she saw the car and recognised her belongings inside. She got inside and decided to drive off in case the thief returned to it. title: How Manchester Pride evolved from a bring-and-buy sale

input.lead: International singers including Ariana Grande and Nelly Furtado have performed at Manchester Pride

input.evidence_text: How Manchester Pride evolved from a bring-and-buy sale - BBC News Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Pride in Manchester began in 1985 from very humble beginnings By Darren Milby Radio Manchester Published 36 minutes ago Manchester Village Pride may look and feel familiar this year but a lot has changed over the past 12 months. The annual event, held over the August bank holiday weekend, hit the headlines in October 2025 when the company behind it went into voluntary administration. Manchester Pride Events LTD owed more than £1m to suppliers and performers. Many of these have still not been paid and the Charity Commission has launched an investigation into the organisation's finances. But how did Manchester Pride reach this point and what does the future hold? Pride in Manchester began in 1985 from very humble beginnings and grew into one of Europe's largest LGBTQ+ festivals attracting more than 170,000 visitors. Big names from the pop world such as Ariana Grande and Nelly Furtado have graced the stage and huge corporate brands were queuing up to have their logos associated with the weekend-long event. This is a world away from the very first Manchester Pride. Image source, Stuart Rhoades Image caption, For more than 40 years, people have gathered in Manchester for the annual event It started with a bring-and-buy sale on Canal Street in the city's Gay Village in 1985. The aim was to raise funds for the ward at Monsall Hospital in north Manchester that was treating patients at the height of the HIV and Aids crisis. The ward looked drab and depressing so fundraisers used the money raised to transform the unit into a welcoming space for patients and their families. Nestled in the village of Cheadle, the gothic building has high-ceilinged rooms, gold chandeliers and a red velvet carpet running down the centre of a large wooden staircase. "She loved the fact that the house had back passageways and staircases that they used to hide from each other." Evers added that the geography of Abney Hall was itself an inspiration. title: Protests and profits: 25 Years of Manchester's second runway

input.summary: We look at the impact the impact of Manchester Airport's second runway 25 years since opening
input.evidence_text: Protests and profits: 25 Years of Manchester's second runway - BBC News Image source, Manchester Airport Image caption, The second runway became operational in 2001 By Judy Hobson , North West Tonight and Jenny Coleman , North West Published 22 August 2026 When Manchester Airport was given permission to build a second runway in 1997 it prompted one of the country's most high-profile environmental protests of the time. Activists from across the country set up camp, built tree houses and a complex network of tunnels in a bid to stop the bulldozers, but after a stand off lasting months they were ultimately evicted and the runway was built. It became operational in 2001 and became the only airport outside of London with two full length runways. Now 25 years on, we look back at the controversy of the project, the impact it has had on the region and its plans for the future. Image source, Manchester Airport Image caption, The airport serves over 32m people each year and connects to more than 200 destinations What were the protests about? Large areas of woodland near to the airport would be need to be removed for the runway to be built. After the plans were approved environmental protesters arrived at the site and set up multiple camps. One of the protestors, Martin Porter who was 27 at the time, was among those that dug tunnels at the site. The protesters were soon joined by a environmental activist named Swampy, real name Dan Hooper. "All the time we were there we had the media, we had Swampy, we were able to give our message that this is a terrible idea, 400 acres of green belt disappearing," Porter said. He had joined the force at 19 after an unhappy two-year stint in the Merchant Navy But becoming a police officer was different. Working the thin blue line suited him – or, as Tony puts it, he was a "round peg" who found a "round hole". Now 72 and long-retired, he joined the force in the early 1970s and eventually worked his way up to sergeant In the late summer of 1989, Tony found himself heading out to a crime scene after his station in Flintshire received the call about a stolen firearm. "I got called to somebody that nicked a shotgun from the back of a car, and some cartridges, and ran off into the woods," he told After witnesses told him which way the thief had fled, he followed the trail through the woodland until he spotted a figure "There's this guy sitting on a stile, and he's got the gun over his knee and a box of cartridges next to him. V News Neal Keeling Chief reporter 07:16, 22 Aug 2026 In his darkest of times Tony Wilson was still capable of a good quote. He was fighting for his life after developing renal cancer when he delivered a memorable quip Doctors had suggested he take Sutent. It would not provide a cure but would extend his life. But Manchester Primary Care Trust refused to fund the £3,500 per month cost of the drug. Yet patients alongside him at The Christie Hospital and living in Cheshire did receive funding Music industry and media friends rallied to help pay. Branding the situation a scandal Wilson pointed out that tummy tucks were available on the NHS, and said at the time: " I thought where am I going to find the money? I'm the one person in this industry who famously has never m He never paid for private health care because he was a socialist. Wilson died on August 10th 2007 aged 57 after the cancer progressed and he suffered a heart attack On his Peter Saville designed headstone in Manchester's Southern Cemetery it says: "Broadcaster Cultural Catalyst". His part in Manchester's renaissance from post-industrial gloom was huge

input.summary: Bolton Council is launching a new licensing scheme for landlords of houses in multiple occupation (HMOs)
input.evidence_text: Bolton Council is launching a new licensing scheme for landlords of houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) The scheme is designed to improve property conditions, strengthen management standards, and ensure tenants have access to safe, high-quality accommodation and was agreed at a meeting of Bolton Council’s Cabinet on Monday (August 17) HMOs are properties that are occupied by three or more people from different households, who share at least one basic amenity i.e. a kitchen, bathroom or toilet - the definition includes bedsits, shared houses and some self–contained flats that did not meet the required standard It is unacceptable that landlords cut corners in critical areas such as failing to obtain fire, gas, and electrical safety certificates or ensuring properties are safe Many landlords operate responsibly, but a substantial proportion of HMOs are poorly managed, unsafe and impact on the community In the past three years, the council has received 1,885 complaints about disrepair in rented homes, typically relating to fire safety, electrical and structural defects, overcrowding, cold and damp, and poor waste management and pest control
